# Diagnosing Persistent Ticking on a 1994 Honda Accord EX

When you adjust valve clearance on an F22B1 engine, silence is the expected outcome. If one cylinder continues to tick after multiple adjustment cycles, it usually indicates that the mechanical relationship between the lifter, cam lobe, and rocker arm has not stabilized as predicted. The scenario describedâwhere a full rotation of the adjustment screw reduces noise significantly but fails to eliminate it entirelyâis a classic diagnostic puzzle.

The most common culprit in this specific configuration is incorrect timing belt alignment during the reassembly phase. On the F22B1, the engine relies on a precise firing order where each cylinder's cam lobes rotate at specific angles relative to the crankshaft. If the timing marks were not perfectly aligned when the valve cover was placed back on, the hydraulic lifters (or solid adjusters, depending on the specific maintenance history) may be sitting on a different portion of the cam lobe than intended. Even if the clearance sounds correct by ear, the geometry might be off enough to cause a "slap" or tick that persists under load.

Another potential issue involves the adjustment technique itself. The method of loosening all valves by roughly 1/4 turn before tightening is a valid strategy used to seat the components evenly without binding them immediately. However, if one specific valve was not fully seated in its bore prior to final tightening, or if the rocker arm pivot bolt was not torqued to specification after the cover installation, the adjustment could be lost under thermal expansion. The fact that the noise persisted for 120 miles suggests the engine has had sufficient time to heat up and cool down multiple times. If the noise remains after these cycles, it is unlikely to be simple "settling."

To determine if the issue lies with the rod bearings versus the valve train, listen closely to the character of the sound. Rod bearing knock typically presents as a deep, metallic rapping that increases in pitch and volume with engine RPM. Crucially, this noise often changes when you tap the engine block or push on various points; if the knock intensifies when you press near the front of the block or the exhaust manifold area, it could suggest the sound is radiating from deeper within the bottom end rather than the top. However, your observation that the sound gets louder when leaning toward the exhaust manifold might also be due to acoustic resonance rather than the source location. In many cases, a ticking sound emanating from the front of the engine bay, near the valve cover, is still indicative of a cylinder head issue, even if you perceive it coming from the side.

If you have confirmed that the timing marks are perfectly aligned and the adjustment was performed with patience, the next step is to isolate the specific lifters. Remove the valve covers and rotate the engine manually one full revolution at a time. Listen for the point where the noise changes pitch or disappears. This will pinpoint exactly which cylinder's cam lobe is not tracking correctly with its corresponding lifter. If the noise persists on a single cylinder despite correct timing, inspect the rocker arm shaft for binding or check if the specific lifter has failed internally.

While mechanical diagnostics are critical, software-based monitoring can also help. Connecting an OBD-II scanner to read engine codes might reveal misfire patterns associated with that specific cylinder. If the ECU detects a cylinder missing its power stroke due to timing issues, it will log a code like P0340 or similar cam/crank correlation errors. This data provides objective confirmation before deciding whether to replace lifters or investigate more catastrophic bottom-end failures.

However, always verify part numbers against the VIN before ordering replacement components.
